Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs. My name is Becky Smith, and I am providing testimony in opposition to LD 1369,
An Act to Provide Emergency Medical Services Training Through the Maine Community College
System.
We appreciate Rep. Fredette's vote of confidence in MCCS' EMS training but cannot provide EMS
training without the appropriate resources to do so. In fact, we already do the training that is contained
within the bill if it is appropriate and allowed within our accreditation.

As this committee heard earlier this session, the Maine Community College System has educated emergency responders for decades and trains a significant number of new responders annually. Our
training centers have been critical partners to the EMS system in Maine. Our collaboration with Maine
EMS, local municipalities and private providers has allowed us to standardize program structure and has
enabled the colleges to align and share curriculum, develop a new curriculum for EMT and Advanced
EMT, share instructors and provide joint instructor training. It has also allowed us to update Training
Center Standards and implement Psychomotor portfolio testing across all programs. We have worked together to expand the training network across the state to ensure the ongoing viability of EMS education, especially in rural areas. The demand for EMS education statewide has never been higher, and this
collaborative approach has been critical in our efforts to help meet those demands, especially in rural areas, and provide equitable access across the state. Six of our colleges and our Harold Alfond Center for
the Advancement of Maine's Workforce now offer some level of EMS training. Our colleges support
high school programs at the CTEs to build a career pathway and engage potential responders early in
their education. We train hundreds of Mainers annually so they can become EMTs or increase their skills
and become Advanced EMTs or Paramedics.
However, EMS training is expensive. This externally accredited training is resource and labor intensive.
At each certification level students complete 12-500 clinical hours in addition to lecture and lab
instruction with a ratio of as few as eight students to one laboratory instructor. A percentage of these
required clinical hours can be met through simulation which has educational benefits, but these sophisticated labs increase equipment costs. Students are also required to complete a range of certifications as well as undergo background checks---AHA, BLS, ALS, et al-- all of which have to be tracked. Moreover, hands-on training uses a significant amount of consumable supplies: this training is
after all replicating real work experiences. These all add up to a significant cost to educate EMS
providers. Moreover, the intentional expansion of training across the state, particularly in rural areas, also
increases the cost. The current cost to educate EMS providers at each level of certification per student is:

TESTIMONY OF REPRESENTATIVE KENNETH W. FREDETTE
IN SUPPORT OF LD 1369
"An Act Providing Emergency Medical Services Training Through the Maine Community College System"
May 5, 2025
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs I Health
and Human Services Senator Rafferty and Representative Murphy, and members of the Committee:
My name is Representative Kenneth W. Fredette, and l represent House District 33 which includes the Town of Newport and surrounding communities. I am pleased to appear before you today as the primary sponsor of LD 1369, "An Act
Providing Emergency Medical Services Training Through the Maine Community College System."
This bill is straightforward in purpose but critically important in impact. It directs
the Maine Community College System to provide no-cost Emergency Medical Senrices (EMS) training, including certification and degree options, within existing
resources.
The Need:
Maine is facing a well-documented and growing shortage of EMS personnel-
both EMTs and paramedics. This crisis is especially acute in our rural and
underserved communities, where EMS providers are aging, overworked, and
under-supported. Recruitment and retention are at crisis levels.
At the same time, too many potential EMS trainees--many of whom are young
Mainers eager to serve their communities---are discouraged by the cost of
certification courses, travel for training, or time away from work.
The Solution: LD 1369 does not create a new program from scratch. Instead, it leverages the
District 33

existing network and capacity of Maine's community college campuses to offer these essential training courses at no cost to the student. The bill is explicitly structured to be implemented within existing resources, respecting our fiscal constraints while empowering our workforce pipeline. This initiative builds on the success of recent tuition-free programs in the trades and healthcare fields. It is aligned with Maine's workforce development goals and will increase both access to training and sen/ice coverage for emergency
response.
The Impact:
By removing financial barriers and offering EMS training locally through our
community colleges, we help meet the critical staffing needs of fire departments,
ambulance sen/ices, and hospitals across Maine. We strengthen public safety
and create new pathways to employment in high-need, high-impact roles.
This is a targeted investment in our people and our communities---and one that will save lives.
Closing:
I respectfully urge the Committee to support LD 1369. Let's ensure that no willing
Mainer is turned away from EMS training due to cost or geography, and that
every town, from Portland to Fort Kent, has the emergency medical professionals
they need.
Thank you for your time, and l would be happy to answer any questions.
District 33
